title: 'Hearken': the first word of the Masnavi
greek: Persian bishnaw ('listen!'); first couplet: bishnaw in nay chun shikayat mikunad / az judaiha hikayat mikunad
short: The Masnavi, Rumi's six-book teaching poem in rhyming couplets, opens with a command to listen, here in E. H. Whinfield's abridged translation (1887; 2nd ed. 1898).
body: Rumi (1207-73) dictated the Masnavi-yi ma'navi ('Spiritual Couplets') at Konya to his disciple Husam al-Din Chelebi over the last fifteen years or so of his life; its opening eighteen couplets are known as the Nay-nama, the 'Song' or 'Book of the Reed'. Whinfield renders each Persian couplet as two English lines, so ll. 1-35 here answer to those eighteen couplets, and the rest of the section to the couplets that follow before the first tale. The very first word, bishnaw, 'listen', marks the whole work as something heard, like the reed's music, rather than read. Nicholson later revised his own rendering of line 1 to follow the oldest Konya manuscript, whose wording differs slightly from the vulgate text. A story in Aflaki's hagiography, that Rumi produced the first eighteen couplets ready-written when Husam al-Din asked him for a poem, is told by Rumi's later hagiographer; Lewis surveys these traditions and their reliability.

title: The reed-flute (nay)
greek: Persian nay
short: The nay, the end-blown reed flute of the Mevlevi ceremony, stands for the human soul, hollowed out and crying for the reed-bed from which it was cut.
body: The nay is a simple end-blown flute cut from a reed; it was Rumi's favourite instrument and became central to the music of the Mevlevi order founded in his name, which still opens its sema ceremony with the flute's solo. Nicholson's Commentary, quoted on the Dar al-Masnavi site, reads the reed as the soul of the perfect man, empty of self so that only the breath of the divine player sounds through it. The flute is also the poet: Rumi speaks through it, and at ll. 52-53 he wishes that the Beloved's lips might touch him so that he too, 'like the flute', would burst into melody. Whinfield's compound 'reed-flute' keeps both the plant and the instrument in view, which matters because the poem moves constantly between the cut stem and the sounding pipe.

title: Complaint and tale
greek: Persian shikayat ('complaint') rhyming with hikayat ('tale, story')
short: The Persian rhymes 'complaint' (shikayat) with 'telling a tale' (hikayat): the reed's lament is also the story the whole Masnavi will tell.
body: In the Persian couplet the reed 'makes complaint' and 'tells a tale of separations' (az judaiha hikayat mikunad), and the two rhyme words differ only in their first consonant. Nicholson's note, quoted by Gamard, takes the mystic's complaint to be in truth a story of endless longing for God, a longing God himself inspires. Whinfield's 'complains' and 'Lamenting its banishment' keep the grief but lose the word 'tale', and with it the hint that the Masnavi's hundreds of stories are all one story of exile and return. His 'banishment from its home' also narrows the Persian plural 'separations' to a single event.

title: 'osier bed': the reed-bed
greek: Persian nayistan ('reed-bed')
short: Whinfield's 'osier bed' (a bed of willows) stands for Rumi's nayistan, the reed-bed: the soul's first home in God, from which it was cut.
body: An osier is a willow used for basket-work (OED, osier n.), so 'osier bed' is an English landscape substituted for a Persian one: Rumi's word is nayistan, literally 'reed-bed'. Nicholson's Commentary, as quoted by Gamard, reads the reed-bed as the soul's original home, its state in Pure Being and Absolute Unity before its descent into the world, to which it longs to return. The image draws on the Sufi idea of the soul's pre-existence and on the Qur'anic Covenant of Alast (Q 7:172), when souls acknowledged their Lord before birth. The violence of the verb, 'they tore me', makes the creation of the instrument a wound: only by being cut does the reed acquire a voice.

title: 'I burst my breast': Whinfield's paraphrase
greek: Persian sina khwaham sharha sharha az firaq ('I want a breast torn shred by shred by separation')
short: Rumi's reed asks for a breast torn to shreds by separation, someone able to hear its pain; Whinfield turns this into the reed bursting its own breast.
body: The Persian couplet means roughly: 'I want a breast torn shred by shred by separation, so that I may explain the pain of longing.' The reed is seeking a listener who has suffered as it has, which prepares for ll. 27-28, where only the 'distracted' can understand. Whinfield's 'I burst my breast, striving to give vent to sighs' makes the reed the one torn open, an image that fits the flute's pierced body but shifts the stress from the listener to the singer. Comparison with Nicholson's more literal version, collected on the Dar al-Masnavi page of translations, shows how freely Whinfield paraphrased; students quoting this text as 'Rumi' should know they are reading a Victorian adaptation.

title: Exile and the return to the root
greek: Persian har kasi k-u dur mand az asl-i khwish / baz juyad ruzgar-i wasl-i khwish
short: Everyone parted from his origin (asl) seeks the time of reunion: the reed's case becomes a law for every soul.
body: The Persian says that whoever remains far from his asl, 'root' or 'origin', seeks again the time of union (wasl) with it; asl and wasl rhyme. Whinfield's 'home' domesticates a philosophical word: the origin is not a place but God, from whom all things come and to whom, in the Qur'anic phrase, they return (Q 2:156, 'to Him we shall return'). This couplet is the hinge where the reed's lament turns into general teaching. Schimmel shows how the motif of the separated part longing for its whole runs through Rumi's imagery, from the drop and the ocean to the exiled nightingale.

title: Each listener hears himself
greek: Persian har kasi az zann-i khwud shud yar-i man / az darun-i man najust asrar-i man
short: Each hearer befriends the reed according to his own opinion, but no one seeks its secrets from within.
body: Literally: 'Each became my friend from his own opinion; none sought my secrets from within me.' The reed plays both at feasts and at funerals (ll. 9-10: 'them that rejoice and them that weep'), and every audience takes the music to mean its own joy or sorrow. The couplet is often read as a comment on the Masnavi itself, which readers have claimed for law-abiding piety, for ecstatic mysticism and for a universal religion of love. Whinfield's 'in harmony with his own feelings' adds a musical pun of his own, since harmony is what each listener fails to reach with the player.

anchor: Body is not veiled from soul
title: Soul, body and the sensual eye
greek: Persian tan zi jan u jan zi tan mastur nist / lik kas ra did-i jan dastur nist
short: The secret is in the sound, yet hidden from the 'sensual eye and ear', as the soul is present in the body and yet unseen.
body: The reed's secret is not separate from its lament, just as the soul is not hidden from the body; yet, the Persian says, no one has been given leave to see the soul. Whinfield's 'sensual eye and ear' renders the outward senses, contrasted throughout the Masnavi with the inward senses of the heart. The analogy is precise: the meaning of the music is in the music, as the soul is in the body, but it needs another kind of perception. Whinfield ends the reed's speech here with a closing quotation mark, although the Persian gives no marks and editors differ on where the reed stops speaking and the poet begins.

title: 'fire, not mere air': Rumi's pun
greek: Persian atash ast in bang-i nay u nist bad / har ki in atash nadarad nist bad
short: Rumi's couplet repeats nist bad, meaning both 'is not wind' and 'may he be nothing': the reed's breath is fire, and whoever lacks it is dead.
body: The two halves of the Persian couplet end on the same words, nist bad. In the first they mean 'is not wind': the reed's cry is fire, not mere breath. In the second they mean 'may he be naught': whoever lacks this fire, let him not exist. This figure, a rhyme on identical words with different senses (tajnis), is untranslatable, and Whinfield splits it between 'not mere air' and 'be accounted dead'. The fire of love (l. 19) answers the 'ferment of love' in wine (l. 20), joining the two great Sufi metaphors of burning and intoxication. Nicholson's Commentary identifies the fire as divine love kindled in the soul.

title: Poison and antidote
greek: Persian hamchu nay zahri u taryaqi ki did?
short: The flute both wounds and heals: its music of separation is a poison that is also the cure, the paradox Sufis saw in love itself.
body: 'Who ever saw a poison and an antidote like the reed?' The taryaq (theriac) was the compound antidote of ancient and Islamic medicine, often made partly from snake flesh, so the pairing is not only paradox but pharmacy. The reed's lament awakens the pain of separation and at the same time consoles it, because it shows that the soul still remembers its source. The medical language returns at ll. 45-47, where Love is hailed as physician, 'our Plato and our Galen'. Schimmel discusses the paired opposites through which Rumi describes love's working.

title: Majnun
greek: Arabic majnun ('possessed, mad')
short: Majnun, the Arab lover maddened by his love for Layla, is the type of the lover who loses reason, the 'distracted' one of l. 27.
body: Qays ibn al-Mulawwah, called Majnun ('mad' or 'possessed by jinn'), is the hero of the Arabic and Persian romance of Layla and Majnun: forbidden to marry his beloved, he wanders the desert reciting poems to her, and Nizami's Persian version (1188) made the story classic. For the Sufis Majnun is the perfect lover, for whom the beloved has replaced the self. Rumi's 'blood-stained path' is the road of love paved with lovers' suffering. The following couplet in the Persian, 'none is the confidant of this sense but the senseless', plays on hush (understanding) and bihush (one who has lost it); Whinfield's 'one distracted' points back to Majnun. The same romance, in Fuzuli's Turkish version, supplies two further poems in this archive ('Mejnun Addresses Nevfil' and 'Mejnun's Gazel').

title: Only the senseless understand
greek: Persian mahram-i in hush juz bihush nist / mar zaban ra mushtari juz gush nist
short: Only one who has lost his ordinary mind can share this knowledge, just as only the ear is a buyer for the tongue's words.
body: The Persian means: 'None is the confidant of this sense but the senseless; the tongue has no customer but the ear.' The first half sets love's understanding against everyday reason, the second gives a homely analogy from the market: words need an ear to buy them. Whinfield's 'As ear inclines to the whispers of the tongue' turns the commercial image into a gentler one. Mahram, the person allowed into the private quarters of a house, makes the knowledge an intimacy reserved for the initiated, and prepares for l. 35, where the 'Raw' cannot understand the 'Ripe'.

title: 'labor and sorrow'
short: The phrase echoes Psalm 90:10, where man's years are 'labour and sorrow'; Rumi's Persian has no biblical echo.
body: Psalm 90:10 (KJV) says of man's threescore years and ten that 'yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.' Whinfield's Victorian readers would probably have heard the Psalm at once, and the echo, whether or not he intended it, gives Rumi's line about days lost in grief the authority of the English Bible. The effect is typical of nineteenth-century translation from Persian, which often reached for biblical diction to signal sacred poetry. The next couplet turns the complaint around: let the days go, so long as 'Thou', the incomparable Pure One, remains.

title: 'Do thou abide'
greek: Persian ruzha gar raft gu ro bak nist / tu bi-man ay an ki chun tu pak nist
short: If the days pass, let them go: what matters is that God, the One without equal in purity, remains.
body: The Persian says: 'If the days have gone, say, Go, there is no fear; do Thou remain, O Thou than whom none is so pure.' The address turns from lament to trust: time is lost, but the eternal beloved is not. Some readers have heard in the address to the 'Pure One' a reference to Shams of Tabriz, Rumi's vanished friend, as well as to God; the Persian supports the theological reading most directly. The archive's 'Yet,,' in l. 31 repeats a comma, a keying slip in the transcription, not part of Whinfield's text.

title: Fish and water
greek: Persian har ki juz mahi z-abash sir shud
short: Only fish never tire of water: only the true lover lives in love without being sated.
body: 'Everyone except the fish has had enough of His water.' The fish is the mystic, whose element is divine love and who therefore cannot have too much of it; others soon want to come up for air. The second half (l. 34) adds that for those without daily bread the day seems long, that is, for those without spiritual sustenance time drags. The fish and the sea become one of Rumi's favourite figures for the soul immersed in God. Schimmel gathers many examples of Rumi's water and fish imagery.

title: 'Raw' and 'Ripe', and the missing half-line
greek: Persian dar nayabad hal-i pukhta hich kham / pas sukhan kotah bayad wa-s-salam
short: The 'raw' (kham) cannot grasp the state of the 'cooked' or 'ripe' (pukhta); Rumi then says 'so the word must be short: farewell', which Whinfield leaves out.
body: Kham and pukhta mean 'raw' and 'cooked' (or 'unripe' and 'ripe'), Sufi terms for the beginner and the mature mystic. Rumi's verse is famous in Persian, and a saying often attributed to Rumi sums up his life as 'I was raw, I was cooked, I was burned'. The couplet's second half, 'so speech must be brief; farewell', closes the eighteen-couplet Nay-nama, and Whinfield drops it: the blank line that follows in the archive marks that gap. The hemistich matters, because it is a deliberate breaking-off: what is beyond the beginner's understanding can only be hinted at.

anchor: pour the ocean into thy pitcher
title: The ocean in a pitcher
greek: Persian gar birizi bahr ra dar kuza'i / chand ganjad qismat-i yak ruza'i
short: Greed is a pitcher that can hold only one day's portion however much ocean is poured into it; only the content oyster fills with pearls.
body: After the Nay-nama Rumi begins to preach. 'Burst thy bonds' (l. 36) urges freedom from silver and gold, and the pitcher image measures desire against need: pour the whole sea into a jug, and it holds only one day's share. The oyster that 'fills not with pearls till it is content' draws on the old belief, common in Persian and Turkish poetry, that pearls form from raindrops received by an oyster that closes upon them (compare the Fuzuli ghazal 'From the Turning of the Sphere' in this archive). Only he 'whose garment is rent by the violence of love', like a mourner or an ecstatic tearing his robe in the sema, is free of greed.

title: Plato and Galen
greek: Persian ay tu Aflatun u Jalinus-i ma
short: Love is hailed as both philosopher and physician: Plato (Aflatun) and Galen (Jalinus), the masters of wisdom and of medicine in Islamic tradition.
body: Greek learning reached Islamic culture through Arabic translation, and Plato (Aflatun) and the second-century physician Galen of Pergamon (Jalinus) were the proverbial authorities of philosophy and medicine. Love, Rumi says, is the 'physician of all our ills' and the cure for our 'pride and self-conceit' (nakhwat u namus): it heals what neither the philosopher's reason nor the doctor's drugs can reach. The salutation 'Hail to thee, then, O LOVE, sweet madness!' renders a Persian line in which love is our 'happy madness' (khwash-sawda), using sawda, the black bile thought to cause both melancholy and passion. Whinfield's capitals for LOVE and BELOVED are his own typographical way of marking the divine sense.

title: Mount Sinai and the swoon of Moses
greek: Persian 'ishq jan-i Tur amad 'ashiqa / Tur mast u kharra Musa sa'iqa
short: Love was the soul of Mount Sinai: when God showed Himself to the mountain it crumbled and Moses fell in a swoon (Qur'an 7:143).
body: In Qur'an 7:143 Moses asks to see God; God answers that he cannot, but tells him to look at the mountain: 'when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble, and Moses fell down in a swoon.' Whinfield quotes this phrase in quotation marks at l. 51. Rumi's Persian makes the mountain drunk (mast) with love and dancing, which links the scene to the dance of l. 49, 'makes the very hills to dance with joy', and so to the Mevlevi whirling. The Persian also has Tur, the Qur'anic name of the mountain, rather than 'Sinai'. Note that the archive's 'O Iover' in l. 50 is a keying slip for 'O lover'.

title: Parted from those of his own tongue
greek: Persian har ki u az hamzabani shud juda / bi-zaban shud gar chi darad sad nawa
short: Whoever is parted from those who share his language becomes dumb, though he have a hundred songs, like the nightingale when the rose is gone.
body: Hamzabani, 'having the same tongue', means sharing a language of the heart, not only Persian or Turkish. Without a sympathetic listener even the most gifted singer falls silent, like the nightingale (bulbul), whose love for the rose is the stock pairing of Persian lyric; when the rose fades its song stops. Readers of Rumi's life often connect these lines with the disappearance of Shams of Tabriz (1248), after which Rumi found other companions, finally Husam al-Din, to whom the Masnavi was dictated. Lewis warns against reading the poem too narrowly as autobiography.

anchor: the rust has not been scoured
title: The rusted mirror
greek: Persian ayinat dani chira ghammaz nist / z-anki zangar az rukhash mumtaz nist
short: The heart is a metal mirror that cannot reflect God until the rust of self has been polished away, a basic Sufi image.
body: Medieval mirrors were polished metal and tarnished quickly. The Sufis took the heart for such a mirror: sin and selfhood rust it, and spiritual discipline and the remembrance of God polish it until it reflects the divine light; a saying ascribed to the Prophet calls remembrance of God the polish of hearts. 'Love desires that this secret should be revealed' explains why the reed speaks at all: a mirror exists to reflect. Whinfield's 'SUN Of GOD' gives the light a capitalised name; readers of Rumi may also hear an echo of Shams al-Din, 'Sun of Religion', the friend whose name the sun imagery of his poetry constantly recalls. Whinfield closes with 'O friends, ye have now heard this tale', the transition to the first story.
